subject: Food Science
title: Emulsions in Food
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Emulsions in Food.

hook.text: Mayonnaise is 80% oil—yet it's creamy, not greasy. The secret is an emulsion that forces oil and water to coexist.

buildup.text: Oil and water don't mix—but emulsifiers (molecules with water-loving and oil-loving ends) stabilize tiny droplets of one within.

discovery.text: Egg yolk lecithin is the classic emulsifier in mayonnaise. Mustard emulsifies.

twist.text: Ice cream is a frozen emulsion—fat droplets in water, stabilized by proteins and polysaccharides—plus air bubbles.

climax.text: Emulsion droplet size determines texture. Smaller droplets feel creamier. Homogenized milk (tiny fat globules) tastes smoother.

punchline.text: Force oil and water together with the right molecule. Droplet size decides if it's creamy.

quiz.question: What makes mayonnaise creamy despite being 80% oil?
options: Lecithin from egg yolk emulsifies oil into tiny stable droplets in water
